cover.headline: North India's diagnostics leader is growing faster again, with no debt and ₹1,700 cr of cash; but at 44.2x FY28E earnings the good news is in the price. On the street's P/E method we see {{dcf.upside|chg}}
cover.lead: Dr Lal PathLabs is India's largest listed pathology chain: 312 labs, 7,727 collection centres and 30 mn patients a year, 75% of revenue from walk-in and home-collection patients, 31% from Delhi NCR and ~77% from North and East India. After three years of 10-12% growth, Q1FY27 revenue rose 19% (patients +8%, revenue per patient +10% incl. a CGHS rate revision) and EBITDA 29% (margin 31%); management now guides 'towards mid-teens' growth. We forecast EPS of ₹39.0 / 44.9 / 51.9 for FY27-29E. Three of the four brokers that disclose a method use **P/E**, and so do we: **45.5x Sep-28E EPS (₹48.4)**, i.e. Dr Lal's 45.7x median one-year-forward P/E since Apr-2021 (on EPS before exceptional items) adjusted -0.6% for the diagnostics peers' move against their own history, gives **{{dcf.tp|inr}} ({{dcf.upside|chg}}): we initiate with HOLD.** Cross-checks: EV/EBITDA ₹2,498; DCF ₹1,128. Bull {{scen.bull.tp|inr}}; bear {{scen.bear.tp|inr}}.

arguments.h: A strong regional franchise, not a national moat
arguments.p: Delhi NCR (31% of revenue, the highest-priced market) still grows double digit; North + East are ~77% of revenue. Brand, density and a hub-and-spoke network give the industry's best margin (~28% before the Q1 spike). Outside the North it has struggled: West slipped to 14% of revenue after the ₹925 cr Suburban deal; South is 6%.

arguments.h: Growth has re-accelerated, partly for one-off reasons
arguments.p: Revenue growth went 10.6% (Q3FY26) → 16.6% → 19.1% (Q1FY27) as new labs matured, Suburban recovered and SwasthFit bundles (27% of revenue) kept growing ~20%. But 2-3pp came from a government (CGHS/ECHS) rate revision that laps in a year, and Dr Lal has not raised list prices for three years. We model +{{F.salesGrowth.0|pct}} / +{{F.salesGrowth.1|pct}} / +{{F.salesGrowth.2|pct}}.

arguments.h: Clean balance sheet, cash looking for a use
arguments.p: No debt, ₹1,693 cr of cash at Jun-2026, negative working capital, capex of ₹140-150 cr a year and a ~45% payout. The cash is earmarked for M&A (SN Genelab ₹168 cr and Ghana ₹38 cr in Sep-2026). Suburban shows that buying growth outside the North is harder than it looks.

arguments.h: Valuation: fair after a 27% rise in a year
arguments.p: At ₹1,987 the stock trades at 44.2x our FY28E EPS against a 45.7x median since 2021. Our 45.5x gives {{dcf.tp|inr}}, a little above the post-Q1 street median (₹2,065), and +11% away: a HOLD on our rule. A 10% growth premium, or the EV/EBITDA analogue of the sector move, would make it a BUY; we explain why we use neither.

catalysts: Q2FY27 results (due by mid-November 2026): whether patient growth holds near 8% through the fever season and the margin stays above 30% as the CGHS benefit is reinvested; any upgrade of the "towards mid-teens" growth guide.
Pricing: management will decide after H1FY27 whether to take the first list-price increase in over three years.
M&A: closing of SN Genelab (expected by 30-Nov-2026) and any larger platform deal in the South or West.
Network: 12-15 new labs and 3-4 radiology centres in FY27; Suburban's return to double-digit growth.
CGHS base effect from Q1FY28; competitive moves by aggregators and hospital labs.

sections.title: What Dr Lal does: collects 95 mn samples a year through 21,000 touch-points and tests them in 312 labs, three-quarters for patients who walk in or book a home visit

blocks.p: Dr Lal PathLabs runs blood, urine and tissue tests (pathology) and a small radiology business (<5% of revenue). In FY26 it served **30.3 mn patients** and processed **94.5 mn samples** (3.1 tests per patient) for **₹2,763 cr of revenue**, i.e. ~₹912 per patient and ~₹292 per sample. Patients reach it in three ways: **7,727 patient service centres** (PSCs: mostly franchised collection centres that take blood and send it on), **13,935 pick-up points** (PUPs: doctors, nursing homes and small labs that hand over samples) and **home collection** booked online or by phone. About **75% of revenue is B2C** (patients paying directly, at list prices) and ~25% B2B (hospitals, institutions, government schemes such as CGHS/ECHS, other labs, at negotiated prices).

**Hub and spoke.** Samples move by courier from the collection points to one of **312 labs**: satellite labs in each city run routine tests (blood counts, sugar, thyroid, lipids) within hours, and complex tests (genomics, oncology, autoimmune, reproductive) go to the **National Reference Lab in Delhi** or the regional reference labs in Kolkata, Bengaluru and Mumbai. The model spreads expensive machines and specialists over a large volume, which is why gross margin is ~81% and EBITDA margin ~28%: the main costs are reagents (19% of revenue), people (18%), fees to collection-centre partners (15%) and logistics, marketing, rent and IT (20%). Routine tests are delivered in 3 hours for ~90% of walk-in patients; ~400 tests are routine (Q1FY27 call).

blocks.callout: **So what:** Dr Lal's economics rest on density. Once a city has a lab, every extra collection centre adds samples at little extra cost; that is why margins are highest in Delhi NCR, where it has been for decades, and why new regions (Mumbai, the South) dilute margins for years. Growth comes from three levers: more patients (network), more tests per patient (bundles, specialised tests) and price (rarely used: no list-price increase in three years).

blocks.callout: **So what:** two distortions run through the history and matter for valuation. (1) COVID: FY22 EPS (₹20.7) was inflated by testing, and FY23 (₹14.3) was depressed by its disappearance plus a full year of Suburban costs. (2) Acquisition accounting: Suburban's brand and customer intangibles cost ₹58 cr of amortisation in FY26 (~₹2.6 of EPS); the brand part ends in FY27, which lifts reported EPS from FY28 without any change in the business. The stock peaked at ₹2,059 in Sep-2021, fell 56% to ₹909 in Mar-2023 and closed at ₹1,987 on 30-Sep-2026.

sections.title: Industry: big, fragmented and growing 8-10% a year; organised chains hold only 15-20%, and competition never lets up

blocks.p: Indian pathology is large and fragmented: over 3 lakh labs, most of them standalone or inside hospitals; organised chains hold only ~15-20% (AR FY26 MD&A). Company slide: standalone centres 42-46%, hospital-based labs 36-40%, diagnostic chains 16-20% (Q1FY27 PPT p.19, 'industry data'). Leading organised players (a CareEdge sample covering ~10-12% of the industry) grew tests from 214 mn (FY21) to 401 mn (FY25) and patients from 64 mn to 99 mn; bundled preventive packages rose from ~6-12% to ~12-25% of their revenue. Urban areas are >70% of diagnostic revenue although >60% of people live in villages. Industry growth is expected at ~8-10% a year over the medium term, mostly volumes (AR FY26 MD&A, citing CareEdge). North and East India lead demand (IMARC, cited in the AR).

blocks.callout: **Pricing is the industry's weak point.** Dr Lal has not raised list prices for over three years and passed on the Q3FY26 GST cut on reagents (12% → 5%); management says competitors have raised prices (JM, Mar-2026) and that pricing is 'neither ... too favorable' nor worse (Q1FY27 call); CGHS/ECHS raised its common rate card in 2026 (2-3% of Dr Lal's revenue). HDFC Securities (Dec-2025): 'test pricing scenario is stable across traditional companies, new-aged ones, and online peers'. The chains grow on volume and mix; when they try to push price, aggregators and hospital labs take the patient.

sections.title: Network and unit economics: revenue = patients × revenue per patient; both levers are working, and the hub-and-spoke keeps ~81% gross margin

blocks.p: Revenue is patients times revenue per patient (RPP). From FY23 to FY26 patients grew only 4% a year (26.9 mn → 30.3 mn) while RPP grew 7% a year (₹750 → ₹912): the growth came from selling more tests per visit (SwasthFit bundles, specialised tests) and from richer mix (Delhi NCR, B2C), not from list prices. In the last three quarters patient growth has stepped up (Q3FY26 +2.7% in a weak fever season, Q4 +8.2%, Q1FY27 +8.2%) as the 32 labs and ~2,000 collection centres added in FY25-26 mature, and RPP jumped 10% in Q1 with the CGHS/ECHS rate revision (2-3pp).

blocks.p: Dr Lal's regional mix has barely moved in three years: **Delhi NCR 31%**, **UP & Uttarakhand 19%**, **rest of North 13%**, **East 15%**, **West 14%**, **South 6%**, others (incl. Nepal and Bangladesh) 2% (FY26). North and East together are ~77%. Delhi NCR is both the largest and the highest-realisation market (B2C, specialised tests); management aims to grow it at double digits, "as near to the overall revenue as possible", and did so in FY26 and Q1FY27. The fastest growth comes from Tier-3-and-below towns, mostly in the North and East, priced like the nearest city cluster: ₹685 cr (FY23) → ₹1,090 cr (FY26), 39% of revenue.

blocks.callout: **Concentration cuts both ways.** It is the source of Dr Lal's margins: dense networks in markets where it is the default choice for doctors. It is also the main strategic risk: a well-funded rival (a hospital chain's lab, an aggregator, a pharma entrant) attacking Delhi NCR would hurt more than any gain elsewhere could offset, and twenty years of trying have not produced a second home market.

sections.title: Suburban Diagnostics: bought for ₹925 cr in 2021 to build the West; a stumble in FY25-26, now recovering, but the West has not grown its share

blocks.p: Agreed 26-Oct-2021, consolidated from 12-Nov-2021: 100% of Suburban Diagnostics (India) Pvt Ltd, Mumbai, for an enterprise value of ₹925 cr (18.5x FY22 EBITDA, floor ₹925 cr, cap ₹1,150 cr), all cash; Suburban had FY21 revenue of ₹294 cr and EBITDA of ₹57.5 cr (incl. COVID testing). Funded partly with a term loan (₹345 cr borrowed in FY22, fully repaid by FY25). Weak for most of FY24-FY26: an IT/LIMS integration and the move of its collection network to franchisees cost revenue for ~3 quarters; West's share of revenue fell from 15% (FY24-25) to 14% (FY26). Voluntarily liquidated into the parent on 18-Mar-2025 (one-time deferred-tax credit ₹40.8 cr in Q4FY25). Q4FY26: 'started picking up'; Q1FY27: 'really turning around ... very close double digits' growth; new stores and radiology centres being opened under the Suburban brand. Profitability no longer reported separately (back end merged); the West's margin is below Delhi NCR's with room to improve (Q4FY26 call).

blocks.callout: **Our read:** Suburban was a sensible, fairly priced attempt to buy a Mumbai brand, but the integration cost a year and the West has not gained share since. The good news is that it now grows again and is fully merged, so the West can be run as one Dr Lal business. The lesson matters for the next deals (SN Genelab, a South platform): Dr Lal's model works best where it is already dense.

sections.title: SwasthFit bundles (27% of revenue) and specialised tests lift revenue per patient; genomics is still small

blocks.p: **SwasthFit** is Dr Lal's range of preventive health packages (a bundle of routine tests at one price, sold to walk-in patients, online and through doctors). It rose from 22% of revenue in FY24 to 24% in FY25 and 27% in FY26, growing ~20% a year, and was 27% again in Q1FY27 (growth ~20%, in line with the company). Bundles raise tests per patient (3.1 in FY26) and are "not margin dilutive" (Q3FY26 call); Suburban's packages are included. They now sell in Tier-2/3 towns as well as metros, sometimes on a doctor's recommendation. **Specialised tests** (genomics, oncology, transplant immunology, autoimmune, reproductive) carry higher prices and higher reagent costs: Dr Lal launched 136 new tests in FY26 (13 first in India) and 116 in Q1FY27, set up specialty verticals (Genevolve for genomics, L-CoRD for reproductive, L-ACE for autoimmune) and hosted a clinician conference (Medllumina). Genomics is still <5% of revenue; SN Genelab (₹58 cr of revenue) would add roughly 2% to group revenue.

Their share has flattened (27% in FY26 and Q1FY27), so the next leg of RPP growth has to come from specialised tests, Delhi NCR mix or price. We assume RPP growth slows from 8% (FY27E, with CGHS) to 6% and 5.5%.

blocks.p: Pricing has been passive: no list-price increase since ~FY23, the Q3FY26 GST cut on reagents (12% → 5%) was passed to patients, and the only price gain in FY27 is the government's CGHS/ECHS rate revision. Management calls price "a strategic lever" and will reassess after H1FY27 depending on "how the pricing table of the competition is moving" and costs; it said competition "has always been intense and is likely to stay intense". A weak rupee and West-Asia freight could raise reagent costs from late FY27 (stock covers 3-4 months).

blocks.callout: **So what:** this is a volume-and-mix business in a market where price is a weapon used by others. A list-price increase of 3-5% after H1FY27 would add ~₹1-2 of EPS a year if volumes hold; we assume only ~1pp of price in FY28E. The bigger risk is the reverse: a renewed discount war in Delhi NCR.

blocks.callout: **Verdict:** A narrow, regional moat: brand and density in North India (Delhi NCR 31% of revenue, North + East ~77%) that gives Dr Lal the industry's best margins and a B2C mix (~75%) that prices above B2B. Low entry barriers and aggregator discounting cap pricing (no list-price increase in three years).

sections.title: Revenue ×2.3 since FY19 and margins back at 28%, but the COVID boom and bust means EPS only regained its FY22 level in FY24

blocks.p: Dr Lal's revenue grew from ₹1,203 cr in FY19 to ₹2,763 cr in FY26 (13% a year), in three phases. **FY20-22: the COVID boom.** RT-PCR testing (₹242 cr of revenue in FY22) and the Suburban acquisition (consolidated from Nov-2021) took revenue up 32% in FY22 and EPS to ₹20.7. **FY23: the bust.** COVID testing fell to ₹25 cr, revenue fell 3%, and a full year of Suburban's acquisition amortisation and loan interest cut EPS 31% to ₹14.3. **FY24-26: steady rebuild.** Organic growth of 10-12%, margins back to 27-28% on operating leverage, and the Suburban loan repaid; EPS ₹21.4 → ₹29.14 → ₹30.13 (₹26.8 and ₹31.6 before a one-time tax credit in FY25 and the labour-code charge in FY26). Over the whole period the business has been remarkably steady underneath: gross margin ~80% and cash conversion above 100% of EBITDA before tax in every year.

blocks.callout: **The Suburban arithmetic.** Dr Lal paid ₹925 cr (18.5x EBITDA) for Suburban in 2021, when its own shares traded at ~72x trailing earnings (Screener), so the deal was cheap relative to Dr Lal's own rating. But the point was to build a second home market in Mumbai and the West, and five years on the West is 14% of revenue, down from 15% in FY24-25 (earlier splits were not retrieved); the company no longer reports Suburban separately, so its return cannot be measured. sections.title: Earnings quality: high: cash-backed profits and a clean audit; read around two one-offs and the acquisition amortisation

bullets: **One-offs:** FY25 profit includes a ₹40.8 cr deferred-tax credit from liquidating Suburban into the parent (8% of profit); FY26 includes a ₹30.1 cr labour-code charge (₹22.5 cr after tax) and a ₹12.2 cr prior-year tax credit. The company's "normalised" PAT was ₹451 cr (FY25) and ₹532 cr (FY26); our base EPS is ₹26.8 and ₹31.6 (reported ₹29.14 and ₹30.13). Screener books the labour-code charge in other income, the company in EBITDA.

**Acquisition amortisation:** ₹57.8 cr in FY26 (~₹2.6 of EPS after tax): the Suburban brand (₹39.2 cr a year) ends in FY27, so reported EPS rises ~₹1.7 in FY28 from accounting alone. We include amortisation in EPS, as the street does.

**Leases (Ind AS 116):** EBITDA excludes rent on ~₹199 cr of leases; right-of-use depreciation (₹40 cr) and lease interest (₹23 cr) are below EBITDA. On a pre-Ind AS basis the FY26 margin would be ~2pp lower (~26%). Peers report the same way.
**ESOP cost:** ₹23.8 cr in FY26 (₹27.1 cr in FY25), expensed inside employee costs; option exercises added ~0.2% to the share count in FY26 (16.718 cr → 16.756 cr shares).
**Cash conversion:** cash from operations before tax was 104-115% of EBITDA in every year FY15-26 (Screener); working capital is negative; receivables 15 days.
**Reclassification:** courier costs moved from employee to other expenses from Q4FY26 (restated); no effect on EBITDA.

**Audit:** Deloitte Haskins & Sells; unmodified opinion; key audit matters are revenue IT controls over the price master (high-volume transactions) and goodwill impairment (₹470 cr in the standalone books from Suburban).

blocks.callout: **Accounting flag: GREEN.** Simple revenue (a test is done, the patient pays), cash ahead of profit, no debt and a conservative auditor's focus on the right risks. The items that distort reported EPS (FY25 tax credit, FY26 labour codes, Suburban amortisation) are disclosed and small; we value on EPS before exceptional items and show reported EPS alongside.

sections.title: Balance sheet: debt-free, ₹1,526 cr of cash and negative working capital; the only liabilities are leases

blocks.p: At Mar-26 Dr Lal held ₹1,526 cr of cash, bank deposits and liquid funds (cash ₹243 cr, other bank balances ₹667 cr, money-market funds ₹423 cr and ₹194 cr of deposits longer than a year) and no borrowings; lease liabilities were ₹199 cr. Net cash after leases was ₹1,328 cr, 4% of the market value. Working capital is negative: patients pay upfront, receivables are ~15 days (mostly B2B and government), inventory is ~30 days of reagents, and suppliers are paid in ~120 days, so growth releases cash. The weak spots are small: ₹548 cr of goodwill and ₹191 cr of intangibles, mostly from Suburban (29% of net worth together), and imported reagents bought from Indian distributors (currency risk, but no dollar debt). On our numbers net cash after leases rises to ₹1,632 / 2,009 / 2,449 cr at Mar-27/28/29 before the SN Genelab and Ghana payments (~₹206 cr).

blocks.h: How the street values Dr Lal

blocks.p: Of the notes standing on 30-Sep-2026 that disclose a method, three value Dr Lal on **P/E** on forward EPS (JM Financial 48x Jun-28E, Nomura 45x Mar-28E, HDFC Securities 44x Q3FY28E) and one on a **DCF** (Emkay, which cross-checks its target at 46-48x FY28E P/E); Kotak, ICICI Securities and 360 ONE do not disclose theirs. We follow the majority: **P/E on Sep-28E EPS (half FY28E, half FY29E)**, the EPS a buyer will look at one year from now. Like the street we value consolidated EPS after minorities (~₹5 cr a year). EV/EBITDA and a DCF are cross-checks.

The house rule (PLAYBOOK §4) starts from the stock's own one-year-forward P/E since Apr-2021, leaving out trough years, and multiplies the median by the sector's move against its own history. Three choices matter here. **(1) Exceptional items.** FY25 EPS includes a ₹40.8 cr one-time tax credit (8% of profit) and FY26 a ₹30.1 cr labour-code charge; as in our recent pharma reports, the base uses **EPS before exceptional items** (forecasts carry none) and the reported-EPS median is a sensitivity. **(2) COVID.** The window includes the FY21-22 testing boom; under §4 a windfall is not a one-off, so reported FY22 EPS stays in, and no year is a trough (below). Prices in Apr-2021 to Mar-2022 were divided by FY23 EPS, the post-COVID low, so those points run at 82-144x; the median is robust to them, but we show the window from Apr-2022 as a sensitivity. **(3) Every weekly close plus the 30-Sep-2026 close** (288 points), median times the sector factor, rounded to the nearest half-turn. No own de-rating, growth or returns adjustment enters the base.

sections.title: Our honest summary: a high-quality, debt-free franchise growing faster again, at a price that already reflects it; HOLD

blocks.callout: **What you are buying:** the leading diagnostics brand in North India, with dense networks that give the industry's best margins, ~75% B2C revenue, negative working capital, no debt and ₹1,700 cr of cash; growth back in the teens on volumes, bundles and a better test mix. **What you are not buying:** pricing power (no list-price increase in three years), a proven model outside the North (Suburban), or protection from aggregator and hospital-lab competition.

**What you are paying:** ₹1,987 is 61.4x trailing EPS, 50.9x our FY27E and 44.2x our FY28E EPS, against a 45.7x median one-year-forward P/E since Apr-2021 (on EPS before exceptional items). The three diagnostics peers trade -0.6% vs their five-year P/E medians; Dr Lal -4.5%. On the street's method (P/E) and our derived 45.5x, the target is {{dcf.tp|inr}} ({{dcf.upside|chg}}): a HOLD. EV/EBITDA (₹2,498) is higher because the sector's EV/EBITDA move is +21.5%; the DCF (₹1,128 at 11.6%) says the price leans on the multiple, as it does for most Indian consumer-healthcare stocks.
